<awtsmoosMeluketTranslation heichel="ikar" alias="meluket_translation_en" seriesId="סיון_meluket" postId="BH_POST_1766518918734_theRebbe_176" batchId="meluket-_D7_A1_D7_99_D7_95_D7_9F_meluket__BH_POST_1766518918734_theRebbe_176__p002">
  <section v="3">
    <sectionSummaryBrief>This section explains that just as the Ten Utterances in action have a general utterance that includes all others, so too in their source in the Sefiros there are levels of general and particular, from Chochmah up through the will before the Tzimtzum.</sectionSummaryBrief>
    <t s="0">And behold, just as it is with the Ten Utterances as they were drawn forth in action and revelation</t>
    <t s="1">(in the Sefirah of Malchus19),</t>
    <t s="2">that the utterance of Bereishis is a general utterance that includes all the utterances,</t>
    <t s="3">so too is it in their source,</t>
    <t s="4">in the Ten Sefiros,</t>
    <t s="5">that the utterance of Bereishis is the general principle,</t>
    <t s="6">and there are several levels to this20.</t>
    <t s="7">For in the Targum Yerushalmi it is stated: "Bereishis — with wisdom21,"</t>
    <t s="8">that Chochmah22</t>
    <t s="9">is the general principle that includes all the Sefiros.</t>
    <t s="10">And in Targum Onkelos it is stated: "Bereishis — in the beginning,"</t>
    <t s="11">and this refers to the will of Kesser that is above Chochmah22,</t>
    <t s="12">and even up to the primordial thought of Adam Kadmon, which is the general will for the entirety of Hishtalshelus,</t>
    <t s="13">and higher still, the will to create worlds as it is before the Tzimtzum,</t>
    <t s="14">which is a level of general principle also relative to the primordial thought of Adam Kadmon.</t>
    <t s="15">And within the Tzimtzum itself there is also general and particular,</t>
    <t s="16">for after it arose in His will, He envisioned within Himself, in potential, all that was destined to be in actuality,</t>
    <t s="17">for the will and the envisioning are levels of general and particular23.</t>
    <t s="18">And it is found,</t>
    <t s="19">that just as the drawing forth of Torah is in the manner of general and particular in many levels,</t>
    <t s="20">as above,</t>
    <t s="21">so too is it in the drawing forth of worlds, which is in the manner of general and particular in many levels.</t>
    <t s="22">And also in this one must understand,</t>
    <t s="23">behold, the intention in the creation of the worlds is that there should be particular creations with division,</t>
    <t s="24">and this intention is the cause for the arousal of the will before the Tzimtzum, in order that from it there should later be drawn forth</t>
    <t s="25">(through the multiplicity of Hishtalshelus)</t>
    <t s="26">ten particular utterances from which particular creations will come into being,</t>
    <t s="27">and if so, it would seemingly have been necessary for the arousal of the will to be from the outset in a particular manner, in a way that it would be possible for the coming into being of particular creations to come from it, in accordance with the intention,</t>
    <t s="28">and why was the arousal of the will initially in the manner of a general principle?</t>
  </section>
  <section v="4">
    <sectionSummaryBrief>This section uses the analogy of a teacher imparting wisdom to a student to explain why the initial influence must be in a concise, general manner, beginning as a point, to ensure proper limitation and alignment with the recipient.</sectionSummaryBrief>
    <t s="0">3)</t>
    <t s="1">And this will be understood through the analogy of the influence of intellect from a teacher to a student,</t>
    <t s="2">for our Sages said24,</t>
    <t s="3">"A person should always teach his student in a concise way,"</t>
    <t s="4">and it is known25</t>
    <t s="5">the precise meaning of the phrase "concise way"</t>
    <t s="6">(and not "a concise intellect"),</t>
    <t s="7">that he must influence the student with all the depth and details that are in the intellect,</t>
    <t s="8">except that all this must be taught to him in a concise way,</t>
    <t s="9">in brief words,</t>
    <t s="10">from which the student can understand all the details.</t>
    <t s="11">And like the Mishnah that our holy Rabbi taught us,</t>
    <t s="12">for in the language of the Mishnah there are</t>
    <t s="13">(in concealment)</t>
    <t s="14">all the details,</t>
    <t s="15">the length, breadth, and depth,</t>
    <t s="16">that are later explained in the Gemara,</t>
    <t s="17">except that in the Mishnah they are in extreme brevity26.</t>
    <t s="18">And the reason for this</t>
    <t s="19">(that the influence must specifically be in a concise way)</t>
    <t s="20">is,</t>
    <t s="21">because if he were to influence him</t>
    <t s="22">(at the outset)</t>
    <t s="23">with all the details in revelation,</t>
    <t s="24">the student's senses would become confused,</t>
    <t s="25">and also it is possible that due to the multiplicity of expansion it would go in a crooked path,</t>
    <t s="26">therefore he must specifically teach him in a concise way,</t>
    <t s="27">for through this the intellect comes in a limited form</t>
    <t s="28">(that he knows the matter in its generality),</t>
    <t s="29">and through this,</t>
    <t s="30">behold, even after he delves into the details,</t>
    <t s="31">with a multiplicity of reasoning,</t>
    <t s="32">the expansion will be according to the manner of the form of the concise words and will not go in a crooked path.</t>
    <t s="33">And just as it is in the actual influence to the student,</t>
    <t s="34">that the beginning of the influence must specifically be in a concise way,</t>
    <t s="35">so too is it in the invention of the intellect that pertains to the student within the teacher himself,</t>
    <t s="36">that the beginning of the drawing forth</t>
    <t s="37">(and invention)</t>
    <t s="38">of the intellect is in the manner of a point.</t>
    <t s="39">For behold, it is known27</t>
    <t s="40">that in the teacher's intellect is also included the externality of the intellect that pertains to the student,</t>
    <t s="41">except,</t>
    <t s="42">that when it is included in the teacher's intellect,</t>
    <t s="43">behold, in addition to it not being discernible there on its own</t>
    <t s="44">(because it is included and mixed with the internality),</t>
    <t s="45">behold, even the externality of the intellect</t>
    <t s="46">(that pertains to the student)</t>
    <t s="47">is in a multiplicity of light,</t>
    <t s="48">therefore the teacher must contract his intellect,</t>
    <t s="49">meaning to conceal his own essential intellect so that it does not shine at all,</t>
    <t s="50">for through this the externality becomes separated from the internality and is discernible on its own,</t>
    <t s="51">and also the externality that is found with him then is only in the manner of a point,</t>
    <t s="52">and only after this</t>
    <t s="53">(before he actually influences)</t>
    <t s="54">does he envision within himself the details that he will influence to the recipient.</t>
    <t s="55">And the reason for this, that initially the intellect comes in the manner of a point, is,</t>
    <t s="56">because if the intellect that pertains to the student were found from the outset in a manner of expansion with a multiplicity of details,</t>
    <t s="57">then the details would be in a manner as they flow from the teacher's intellect,</t>
    <t s="58">in a multiplicity of light,</t>
    <t s="59">and they would not be directed and suited to the student's senses.</t>
    <t s="60">Therefore,</t>
    <t s="61">the invention of the intellect initially is in the manner of a point</t>
    <t s="62">(a matter of concealment),</t>
    <t s="63">for through this the intellect becomes bounded.</t>
    <t s="64">For despite the fact that in the point are included all the details that he will later influence to the student</t>
    <t s="65">[and moreover,</t>
    <t s="66">that in the point there is also, in concealment, from the internality of the intellect28],</t>
    <t s="67">nevertheless,</t>
    <t s="68">since all this is in concealment,</t>
    <t s="69">behold, through this a boundary and form</t>
    <t s="70">(general)</t>
    <t s="71">is made in the intellect, so that it will be in a manner that is fit to be influenced to the student,</t>
    <t s="72">and after this boundary is made in it,</t>
    <t s="73">behold, even after it is drawn forth in breadth and expansion</t>
    <t s="74">(when he specifies the details),</t>
    <t s="75">the breadth will be according to the manner of the boundary and form of the point.</t>
  </section>
  <section v="5">
    <sectionSummaryBrief>This section applies the analogy above to the Divine realm, explaining that the initial drawing forth of light from Ein Sof had to be in a general manner to create a bounded form suitable for the worlds, so that subsequent details would also be within that measure.</sectionSummaryBrief>
    <t s="0">4)</t>
    <t s="1">And the analogue from this will be understood Above,</t>
    <t s="2">that in order for the light that brings worlds into being to be commensurate with the creatures,</t>
    <t s="3">in a way that it can shine within them internally,</t>
    <t s="4">it was necessary that there first be a drawing forth in the manner of general and particular.</t>
    <t s="5">For since the worlds are incomparable relative to the Ein Sof light,</t>
    <t s="6">therefore,</t>
    <t s="7">if the drawing forth from Ein Sof were from the outset in a multiplicity of details,</t>
    <t s="8">then the details would be without limit</t>
    <t s="9">(as they are from the perspective of Ein Sof),</t>
    <t s="10">therefore it was necessary that there first be a drawing forth in the manner of a general principle,</t>
    <t s="11">for through this a general form is made in the light, so that it will be commensurate with the worlds,</t>
    <t s="12">and through this,</t>
    <t s="13">even the details that are drawn forth afterward are according to this form.</t>
  </section>
</awtsmoosMeluketTranslation>
